meta.description: Native Everglades species that are not federally listed as endangered or threatened, including the recovered American alligator. Used by the Identify page and the AI Guide.

species.summary: A large, dark reptile of freshwater marshes and canals that digs 'gator holes' other wildlife depend on in the dry season.
species.description: The American alligator lives in freshwater across the Southeast, and the Everglades is one of its strongholds. Alligators were once close to disappearing from overhunting, but protection helped them recover. They are still protected by federal and Florida law, partly because they look so much like the rarer American crocodile. In the dry season, alligators dig and clear holes in the marsh that hold water, which gives fish, turtles, and wading birds a place to survive.
species.habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, lakes, rivers, and canals.
threats: Water-level changes that can flood nests or dry out the pools they depend on
People feeding alligators, which makes them lose their natural wariness
Vehicle collisions on roads near water
identification_tips: Broad, rounded, U-shaped snout (crocodiles have a narrow, V-shaped one)
Dark gray to black body, often with pale bands on young animals
Only the upper teeth show when the mouth is closed
Large adults commonly reach 8 to 12 feet or more
how_to_help: Never feed alligators; it is illegal in Florida and makes them dangerous
Keep a safe distance, and keep pets and children away from the water's edge
Report a nuisance alligator to FWC's alligator hotline at 866-FWC-GATOR (866-392-4286)
Support protection and restoration of Everglades wetlands

species.summary: A flat, leathery-shelled turtle with a long snout that often hides in mud and waits for prey.
species.description: The Florida softshell is a large freshwater turtle. Its shell is covered in soft, leathery skin instead of hard plates, which helps it move quickly through water. It spends most of its time in the water, often buried in mud or sand with only its long neck and snout showing, and it eats fish, frogs, insects, and other small animals.
species.habitat: Freshwater lakes, canals, ponds, and slow rivers and marshes with soft, muddy bottoms.
threats: Cars hitting females as they cross roads to nest
Loss of wetlands and nesting areas
identification_tips: Flat, round, olive-to-brown shell with a soft, leathery edge and no hard plates
Long neck and a long, tube-shaped snout
Webbed feet with three claws on each foot
how_to_help: Do not pick up or take a softshell; they can bite and reach far with their long necks
Drive slowly near canals and wetlands, especially in nesting season
Pick up fishing line and hooks and throw them away properly
Keep canal banks and nesting areas natural

species.summary: A tall wading bird that stands still in shallow water and strikes fish with its long bill.
species.description: The great blue heron is a common wading bird across Florida and the Everglades. It stands motionless or walks slowly through shallow water, then spears fish, frogs, and other small animals. Herons nest in colonies in trees and shrubs, and like most native birds they are protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. South Florida is also home to an all-white form often called the great white heron.
species.habitat: Freshwater and saltwater shallows, marshes, mangroves, canals, ponds, and shorelines.
threats: Loss of wetlands and shallow feeding areas
Tangling in fishing line and hooks
Pollution that harms the fish they eat
identification_tips: Very tall wader, about 4 feet high, with a wingspan around 6 feet
Blue-gray body with a white face and a black stripe over the eye
Long yellowish bill and long legs
Flies with its neck folded back in an S shape
A white form lives in south Florida
how_to_help: Keep your distance from nests and feeding birds
Throw away fishing line and hooks so birds cannot get tangled
Do not feed herons or leave fish scraps at docks
Protect wetlands and keep canals clean
